Meeting of 28-29 October 2026
Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday, 28-29 October 2026
26 November 2026
1. Review of financial, economic and monetary developments and policy options
Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started her presentation on the latest financial market developments with the observation that higher energy prices since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 September 2026 had reinforced concerns about persistent inflationary pressures. At the same time, market attention had shifted towards fiscal dynamics and concerns about the increasingly debt-financed artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle. 
Energy price pressures had intensified substantially since the September meeting, pushing oil and gas prices above the adverse scenario of the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In response to renewed tensions in the Middle East, the latest oil futures curve had shifted markedly higher compared with the baseline of the September projections and had also moved visibly above the adverse scenario over the short term. The repricing in gas markets had been even more pronounced, with the futures curve currently standing well above the adverse scenario over the entire horizon. 
Diesel refining margins stood at a historically high level, with euro area diesel crack spreads – the differences between wholesale prices and crude oil prices – above the levels observed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Freight rates from the Gulf region to Europe had surged to record highs, while the probability of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 was at its lowest since the start of the war in the Middle East. The increase in energy prices was reflected in inflation compensation. Inflation fixings throughout 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and remaining above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028, while inflation fixings for 2028 were broadly unchanged. Option-implied inflation risks continued to be skewed to the upside over the next two years and five years. 
Despite the sharp increase in energy prices and the deterioration in the inflation outlook, expectations for the key ECB interest rates stood near their September levels. The one-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate one year ahead had decoupled from energy prices, consistent with communication that interest rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Immediately after the Governing Council’s September monetary policy meeting, the OIS forward curve had shifted markedly higher, temporarily pricing in more than four additional 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months, before investors pared back expectations to just under three additional hikes. Market pricing adjusted for term premia pointed to an expected peak in the deposit facility rate at around 3%, implying a more pronounced tightening than the median expectation of participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts, which foresaw only one more hike. 
Euro area risk-free rates had stabilised and, at longer tenors, had even declined since the September meeting, while US rates had risen across maturities on the back of higher real rates. The divergence between real yields in the euro area and the United States was consistent with investors’ perceptions of a more dynamic US economy.
The rise in euro area ten-year rates relative to the average in 2024 had been driven primarily by higher real term premia, reflecting increased uncertainty about the long-run macroeconomic outlook and a growing net supply of public and private debt. Higher expected short-term real rates and higher inflation expectations accounted for around one-third of the increase in ten-year rates. Moreover, the shift in stock-bond correlations into positive territory pointed to reduced diversification benefits from bonds amid more frequent adverse supply shocks, requiring greater compensation to hold duration risk.
As higher real rates raised governments’ borrowing costs and reduced fiscal space, sovereign bond yields had become more sensitive to differences in the fiscal outlook. Sovereign bond spreads had increased notably for some countries since the previous monetary policy meeting, but they had generally remained well below earlier peaks and broadly in line with fundamentals. A greater responsiveness of euro area sovereign bond yields to market stress also reflected a shift towards more price-sensitive investors. Despite the recent widening in spreads, systemic stress indicators had remained contained, well below levels recorded in previous episodes of market strain. 
Euro area bank equities had overall remained resilient and, despite a recent correction, had continued to trade in positive territory over the year to date, benefiting from the higher interest rate environment and banks’ solid profitability and strong capital positions. Euro area banks had continued to reduce their domestic exposures in total government bond holdings. This suggested that they were less exposed to domestic shocks, as portfolios had become more diversified.
Concerns about inflation, financial conditions and fiscal policy had also extended to broader equity markets, with euro area stocks underperforming. A further factor weighing on equity markets globally had been the sharp correction in tech stocks, as growing concerns about the increased debt financing of the AI build-out and the returns it would generate had caused significant volatility. The substantial increase in debt issuance by hyperscalers to finance AI investment had so far been smoothly absorbed in euro area corporate bond markets, but at a higher cost for issuers. 
Weakening risk sentiment towards the euro area and diverging interest rates had been reflected in the EUR/USD exchange rate, which had depreciated noticeably since the September meeting. Overall, financial conditions had tightened recently, mainly owing to a correction in risk assets and higher sovereign yields, although partly offset by the weakening of the exchange rate. 
Ms Schnabel then turned to short-term funding markets. Bank borrowing costs in overnight repo markets had continued their gradual upward trend, with the spreads between rates for French, Italian and Spanish collateral broadly stable against those using German collateral. Liquidity redistribution across banks had continued to operate smoothly, with money market conditions adjusting well to an environment with less excess liquidity. On 27 October 2026, recourse to the Eurosystem’s standard refinancing operations had risen to its highest level since the end of 2016, with short-term money market rates remaining close to the deposit facility rate. Both the seven-day main refinancing operation, which covered the October 2026 month-end, and the three-month longer-term refinancing operation, which covered the 2026 year-end, had contributed to the increase. Overall, this was a comforting sign that banks were becoming more accustomed to using standard refinancing operations in their day-to-day liquidity management as balance sheet normalisation and the reduction of excess liquidity progressed.
The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane then went through the latest economic, monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area.
Starting with inflation in the euro area, Mr Lane noted that headline inflation, as measured by the Harmonised index of Consumer Prices (HICP), had risen to 3.8% in September, from 3.2% in August. This increase had been driven by energy price inflation, which had increased markedly to 18.9% from 14.3%. Diesel and petrol prices had reached new peaks in September, in part reflecting elevated refining margins. Inflation excluding energy had risen to 2.3% in September, from 2.1% in August. Food inflation had increased by 0.2 percentage points in September, to 1.3%, in part owing to the impact of the summer heatwaves on the unprocessed food component. Core inflation (HICP inflation excluding energy and food) had edged up to 2.5% in September, from 2.4% in August: a 0.1 percentage point decline in goods inflation to 1.1% had been offset by a 0.2 percentage point increase in services inflation to 3.2%. 
The pass-through of the energy shock to inflation remained most visible in direct effects. Indirect effects had, overall, evolved as expected and were still limited. So far there had been no material signs of second-round effects. Indicators of underlying inflation had remained broadly stable and wage pressures remained moderate. Compensation per employee had grown by 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% in the first quarter, while rising productivity had helped contain the growth of unit labour costs. At the same time, the early stages of the pricing chain pointed to upward pressures. The ECB’s forward-looking wage tracker suggested that negotiated wage growth would fluctuate between 2.5% and 2.8% in the remaining months of 2026 and average 2.6% in the first three quarters of 2027, broadly in line with the September staff projections. However, in the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) input prices had picked up to 67.3 in October, from 67.0 in September and 62.8 in August. In addition, the selling price expectations of firms over the coming year had increased in the latest round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area. These signals suggested that indirect and second-round effects would become more material over time, as anticipated in the September staff projections.
Market and survey-based inflation expectations over shorter horizons had risen, but most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stood at around 2%, supporting the stabilisation of inflation around target in the medium term. Estimates of market-implied inflation expectations (derived from measures of inflation compensation by adjusting for risk premia) averaged 3.1% for 2026, 3.3% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028. Expectations of professional forecasters for headline inflation had been revised up for 2027 but were unrevised for 2028 at 2.0%. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations of consumers were broadly stable, as were expectations of firms, according to the second quarter and third quarter rounds of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises. 
Brent crude oil prices (front month – based on futures) had increased by 13% to USD 115 per barrel since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting, in an environment of heightened volatility, elevated freight rates and high global prices for refined products. Price pressures had been particularly pronounced for physical Brent contracts, which reflected prices for more immediate delivery than the front-month prices. Gas prices had increased by 22% to €97 per MWh over the same period, owing to upward pressure from the Middle East conflict. The euro had depreciated by 4.0% against the US dollar since the September meeting, and by 2.2% in nominal effective terms. 
The incoming information pointed to continued global economic growth in the third quarter, with the global composite output PMI (excluding the euro area) increasing to 54.5 in September, reflecting expansion in both the manufacturing and services sectors. At the same time, stocks of finished goods had increased to well above their long-term averages, suggesting some hoarding of finished goods to insulate against persis

Record of the Financial Policy Committee meeting on 19 November 2026
Headline judgements and policy actions
Overall summary
Since the July Financial Stability Report (FSR), the conflict in the Middle East has continued to disrupt global energy markets and supply chains; concerns about sovereign debt sustainability have intensified; and there have been repeated swings in investors’ expectations about the future earnings of artificial intelligence (AI) companies. These developments have contributed to higher expected policy rates, higher bond yields and volatility in financial markets. Some market moves have been amplified by vulnerabilities previously identified by the Financial Policy Committee (FPC).
Despite some amplification within markets, spillovers across markets have been limited and the UK financial system has been resilient. AI investment has supported global growth. However, the very rapid expansion and broadening of its financing – in a form that is increasingly complex, circular and opaque – is also contributing to a deepening of interconnections across the global financial system, making it increasingly likely for stress in one area to propagate to another. Alongside this, the higher interest rate and cost environment is eroding financial headroom for some households and adding to sovereign debt sustainability pressures. Taken together, these developments heighten the risk that multiple vulnerabilities crystallise simultaneously. 
Meanwhile, frontier AI capabilities have continued to grow since the July FSR, notably in the sophistication of AI agents and open-weight AI models. Recent incidents have further illustrated the challenges in aligning and controlling both individual agents and multi-agent dynamics. These developments are making cyber and operational risks a more prominent threat to financial stability, and are contributing to deeper interconnections across the financial system through common technologies and providers.
Global risk environment
The continued conflict in the Middle East has led to a protracted negative supply shock to the global economy. Energy prices have increased since the July FSR, adding to inflationary pressures and contributing to higher interest rates. The outlook for inflation and interest rates remains uncertain and sensitive to developments in the Middle East and their impacts.
Global growth has so far been resilient, in part supported by AI-related investment. This investment also increases the demand for capital which may be contributing to upward pressure on global real interest rates. Uncertainty over the pace of data-centre development, and how much AI investment will translate into future earnings, has contributed to asset price volatility.
Financial vulnerabilities
Vulnerabilities previously highlighted by the FPC in sovereign debt markets, risky asset valuations, and risky credit markets including private credit, remain and, in some cases, have amplified market volatility.
Sovereign debt-to-GDP ratios continue to move upwards globally, reducing the capacity of governments to respond to future shocks. Government bond yields have risen further, reaching near two-decade highs in several advanced economies. In the UK, the increase in yields has mainly reflected higher expected policy rates, driven by higher energy prices and resilient growth, rather than higher term premia. Fiscal and political uncertainty have contributed more materially to increases in yields in some other countries, particularly France. Many sovereign bond markets are characterised by a relatively high use of leverage by hedge funds pursuing similar trading strategies across jurisdictions. Market intelligence suggests that deleveraging by hedge funds contributed to the increase in French sovereign bond yields. Spillovers from French sovereign bonds to other markets, including gilts, have been limited.
UK gilt and gilt repo markets have functioned well, with gilt bid-offer spreads remaining within historical norms. Hedge fund leverage remains elevated by historical standards, although net repo borrowing has declined somewhat since July. In a severe stress, deleveraging by highly leveraged market participants could amplify market moves, impair market functioning and transmit stress back to banks providing financing to these participants. Although the gilt repo market has been resilient recently, past episodes of market dysfunction have highlighted the importance of reforms to ensure the resilience of this market in stress (see Box A of the FSR).
Equity valuations remain stretched on some measures, despite recent falls, with valuations of AI and technology-related companies embedding strong expectations for future earnings. Leveraged funds and retail investors remain exposed to AI stocks, with hedge funds also obtaining leverage through significant prime brokerage borrowing. The value of AI-related equities fell sharply following the US midterm elections, as investors re-assessed the scale, pace and cost of AI-related investment. These moves were amplified by some hedge funds deleveraging. Recent volatility in South Korean equity markets has also provided evidence that procyclical rebalancing by leveraged exchange-traded funds can amplify falls in equity prices. While spillovers to other markets were limited across these episodes, in a more severe shock, losses on equity positions could also lead globally active investors to deleverage in other markets, including sovereign debt markets.
Higher borrowing costs have increased refinancing pressures in corporate debt markets, particularly for weaker borrowers. Spreads widened sharply for US CCC-rated debt and for some lower-quality AI-related borrowers. Spread widening across higher-rated corporate debt has been more limited. There are some signs of increasing stress in parts of private credit, though vulnerabilities have not materially changed overall and stress remains more contained among UK borrowers. A further tightening in risky credit markets could increase financing costs for UK businesses and amplify the impact of an adverse shock.
AI-related financing has grown rapidly and is increasingly spanning equity markets, public bond markets, private credit and more complex financing structures. This is increasing interconnections across the financial system, making it more likely for stress in one area to propagate to another. Hyperscaler bond issuance is set to exceed $305 billion in 2026, accounting for around 8% of global investment grade issuance, with the share rising considerably when considering the broader AI-related issuer ecosystem. Some AI-related companies are also providing finance to others in the sector to support investment, in arrangements linked to future revenue commitments, strengthening sectoral interconnections. Greater use of debt financing could increase the potential for losses in the financial system, while more complex structures and circular financing arrangements can make it more difficult to identify concentrations of risk and where exposures ultimately sit.
Operational vulnerabilities
Firms will need to keep pace with the growing scale and sophistication of cyber threats, including by ensuring that any deployment of frontier AI to identify and remediate cyber threats is undertaken safely, while accelerating long-term preparations for quantum-resistant cryptography. They will also need credible arrangements to recover quickly from operational disruption, in order to maintain the provision of vital financial services. Taken together, these will place competing demands on technology skills and management capacity. A failure to take action will compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications.
Frontier AI capabilities have continued to grow since the July FSR, notably in the sophistication of AI agents and open-weight AI models. Recent incidents have further illustrated the challenges in controlling the risk that increasingly autonomous AI agents act in ways that are misaligned with the objectives intended by developers and users. Separately, the rapid development of open-weight AI models that could be run more cheaply than proprietary models, with safeguards more easily disabled or removed, can make advanced AI models more readily available and useful to malicious actors.
In addition, recent Google Cloud and Microsoft outages have illustrated how operational dependencies mean disruption at a single provider can affect many firms at once. Firms increasingly rely on common technologies and third-party providers, and growing AI adoption deepens these dependencies and creates new ones. This underlines the importance of continuing to operationalise the UK’s critical third party (CTP) regime.
The FPC underlines the importance of firms engaging with guidance from regulatory authorities, such as the joint consultation paper published on 19 November by the Bank, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority on Cyber Risk and Resilience Management, with proposals for a set of principles-based and outcomes-focused expectations for regulated firms and FMIs to strengthen their cyber risk and resilience. The FPC also notes the importance of sector-wide collaboration in helping firms address emerging frontier AI risks and ensuring the system continues to deliver vital financial services throughout operational incidents.
Further ahead, quantum computing could compromise widely used cryptography and hence cyber security. This makes an orderly transition to quantum-resistant cryptography a priority and has implications for actions and decisions firms have to take now.
Overall, the FPC judges that the evolving operational risk environment reinforces the need for significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience.
UK household, corporate and banking system resilience
UK household and corporate balance sheets remain strong in aggregate, supported by stronger than expected GDP growth, but financial headroom is being eroded across borrowers, with some households more affected than others. Successive interest-rate and cost shocks are reducing the capacity of some households to absorb further shocks. Businesses are facing higher costs and tighter financial conditions. Pressures are greatest for small and medium-sized enterprises, energy-intensive firms and highly leveraged corporates, particularly where exposure to higher energy costs, limited financial buffers and refinancing needs overlap.
The UK banking system remains well capitalised with high levels of liquidity, and impairments remain low. The banking system therefore has the capacity to support households and businesses even if economic and financial conditions were to be substantially worse than expected. Despite heightened uncertainty, banks have continued to support lending to the real economy – aggregate gross lending to UK households and businesses in 2026 Q3 was 9% higher

Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement 
On November 24, 2026, NXP B.V., NXP Funding LLC, NXP USA, Inc. (the “Issuers”) and NXP Semiconductors N.V. (the “Company”) completed an underwritten public offering of €500,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 4.625% Senior Notes due 2034 (the “2034 Notes”) and €500,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 4.875% Senior Notes due 2037 (the “2037 Notes” and, collectively with the 2034 Notes, the “Notes”). The Notes were offered and sold pursuant to the Issuers’ and the Company’s automatic shelf registration statement on Form S-3ASR (Registration No. 333-289512), which was filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) and became effective on August 12, 2025. 
The Company and the Issuers intend to use the net proceeds from the offering of the Notes for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures or debt repurchases or repayments. 
The Notes were issued pursuant to an indenture, dated as of May 16, 2022 (the “Base Indenture”), among the Issuers, the Company, as guarantor, and Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by the third supplemental indenture, dated as of November 24, 2026, among the Issuers, the Company, as guarantor, and the Trustee (the “Third Supplemental Indenture” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”). Interest is payable on the 2034 Notes annually in arrears at an annual rate of 4.625% on February 24 of each year, beginning on February 24, 2027. The 2034 Notes will mature on February 24, 2034. Interest is payable on the 2037 Notes annually in arrears at an annual rate of 4.875% on November 24 of each year, beginning on November 24, 2027. The 2027 Notes will mature on November 24, 2037. 
At any time prior to (i) November 24, 2033 (the date three months prior to the maturity date of the 2034 Notes) for the 2034 Notes and (ii) August 24, 2037 (the date three months prior to the maturity date of the 2037 Notes) for the 2037 Notes (collectively, the “Par Call Dates”), the Issuers may redeem the applicable series of Notes, in whole or in part, at a price equal to the greater of (i) 100% of the principal amount of the Notes to be redeemed and (ii) the sum of the present values of the remaining scheduled payments of principal and interest to the applicable Par Call Date discounted to the applicable date of redemption (assuming the Notes matured on the applicable Par Call Date) on an annual basis at the Comparable Government Bond Rate (as defined in the Third Supplemental Indenture), plus 20 basis points in case of the 2034 Notes and 25 basis points in case of the 2037 Notes, plus, in each case, any accrued and unpaid interest thereon. The Issuers may redeem a series of Notes, in whole or in part, at any time and from time to time, on or after the applicable Par Call Date for such series of Notes at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to, but excluding, the date of redemption. 
If the Issuers experience specific kinds of changes of control, they will be required to offer to purchase each series of the Notes at a purchase price equal to 101% of the principal amount, plus accrued and unpaid interest. If holders of not less than 90% in aggregate principal amount of a series of Notes then outstanding validly tender and do not withdraw such Notes in an offer to purchase and the Issuers, or any third party making such an offer in lieu of the Issuers as described below, purchase all of such Notes properly tendered and not withdrawn by such Holders, the Issuers or such third party will have the right, upon not less than 10 days’ nor more than 60 days’ prior notice (provided that such notice (the “Second Change of Control Payment Date”) is given not more than 60 days following such repurchase pursuant to the offer to purchase described above) to redeem all Notes of such series that remain outstanding following such purchase on a date specified in such notice and at a price in cash equal to 101% of the aggregate principal amount of the Notes repurchased plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, on the Notes repurchased to, but excluding, the Second Change of Control Payment Date. 
The Notes will be senior unsecured obligations of the Issuers and will be guaranteed by the Company on a senior unsecured basis (the “Guarantee”). The Notes and the Guarantee will rank equal in right of payment with all of the Issuers’ and Company’s existing and future senior unsecured indebtedness, but will be effectively junior to all of the Issuers’ and the Company’s future secured indebtedness to the extent of the value of the assets securing such indebtedness and effectively junior in certain circumstances to indebtedness incurred under NXP B.V. and NXP Funding LLC’s Revolving Credit Facility with respect to certain assets of NXP B.V. and its subsidiaries in the event that such assets may secure such indebtedness in the future. The Notes and the Guarantee will rank senior in right of payment to the Issuers’ and the Company’s existing and future subordinated indebtedness and will be structurally subordinated to all of the liabilities, including trade payables, of their subsidiaries. 
The Indenture provides for customary events of default, including failure to make required payments; failure to comply with certain agreements or covenants; failure to pay, or acceleration of, certain other material indebtedness; certain events of bankruptcy and insolvency; and failure to pay certain judgments. An event of default under the Indenture will allow either the Trustee or the holders of at least 30% in aggregate principal amount of the then outstanding Notes of the applicable series to accelerate the amounts due under the Notes.

On November 25, 2026, American Tower Corporation (the “Company”) completed a registered public offering of €600.0 million aggregate principal amount of its 4.200% senior unsecured notes due 2031 (the “2031 notes”) and €600.0 million aggregate principal amount of its 4.500% senior unsecured notes due 2034 (the “2034 notes” and, together with the 2031 notes, the “Notes”), which resulted in aggregate net proceeds to the Company of approximately €1,191.3 million (approximately $1,317.0 million at the euro/U.S. dollar exchange rate of €1.00 = $1.1055, as reported by Bloomberg on November 12, 2026), after deducting commissions and estimated expenses. The Company intends to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, including but not limited to refinancing upcoming euro maturities. 
The Company issued the Notes under an indenture dated as of June 2, 2025 (the “Base Indenture”), between the Company and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by a supplemental indenture dated as of November 25, 2026 (the “Supplemental Indenture No. 4” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”), among the Company, the Trustee and U.S. Bank Europe DAC, UK Branch, as paying agent. The following description of the Indenture is a summary and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the detailed provisions of the Indenture. 
The 2031 notes will mature on February 20, 2031 and bear interest at a rate of 4.200% per annum. The 2034 notes will mature on February 20, 2034 and bear interest at a rate of 4.500% per annum. Accrued and unpaid interest on the Notes will be payable in euros in arrears on February 20 of each year, beginning on February 20, 2027. Interest on the Notes will accrue from November 25, 2026 and will be computed on the basis of the actual number of days in the period for which interest is being calculated and the actual number of days from and including the last date on which interest was paid on the Notes. The terms of the Indenture, among other things, limit (a) the Company’s ability to merge, consolidate or sell assets, and (b) the Company’s and its subsidiaries’ abilities to incur liens. These covenants are subject to a number of exceptions, including that the Company and its subsidiaries may incur liens on assets, mortgages or other liens securing indebtedness, provided the aggregate amount of indebtedness secured by such liens shall not exceed 3.5x Adjusted EBITDA as defined in the Indenture. 
The Company may redeem the Notes at any time, in whole or in part, at its election at the applicable redemption price. If the Company redeems (a) the 2031 notes prior to January 20, 2031, or (b) the 2034 notes prior to December 20, 2033, the Company shall pay a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed plus a make-whole premium, together with accrued interest to the redemption date. If the Company redeems (a) the 2031 notes on or after January 20, 2031, or (b) the 2034 notes on or after December 20, 2033, the Company shall pay a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed plus accrued interest to the redemption date. In addition, if the Company undergoes a Change of Control and Ratings Decline, each as defined in the Indenture, the Company may be required to repurchase all of the Notes at a purchase price equal to 101% of the principal amount of the Notes, plus accrued and unpaid interest (including additional interest, if any), up to but not including the repurchase date. 
The Indenture provides that each of the following is an event of default (“Event of Default”): (i) default for 30 days in payment of any interest due with respect to the Notes; (ii) default in payment of principal or premium, if any, on the Notes when due, at maturity, upon any redemption, by declaration or otherwise; (iii) failure by the Company to comply with covenants in the Indenture or Notes for 90 days after receiving notice; and (iv) certain events of bankruptcy or insolvency with respect to the Company or any of its Significant Subsidiaries, as defined in the Indenture. If any Event of Default arising under clause (iv) above occurs, the principal amount and accrued and unpaid interest on all the outstanding Notes will become due and payable immediately without further action or notice. If any other Event of Default occurs and is continuing, the Trustee or the holders of at least 25% in principal amount of the then outstanding Notes may declare the entire principal amount on all the outstanding Notes to be due and payable immediately. 
The foregoing is only a summary of certain provisions and is qualified in its entirety by the terms of the Base Indenture, as filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) on June 2, 2025 as an exhibit to the Company’s Registration Statement on Form S-3 (No. 333-287714), and the Supplemental Indenture No. 4, a copy of which is filed herewith as Exhibit 4.1, and incorporated by reference herein.

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 
Federal Reserve Board

The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). 
By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. 
Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500. 
The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026. 
The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases.

PRESS RELEASE
ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
25 November 2026
Agreement paves way for settlement of large-value payments in Swedish kronor using T2
Migration targeted for February 2030
The European Central Bank (ECB) and Sveriges Riksbank have concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. Today, ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen took part in a signing ceremony for the T2 currency participation agreement at the ECB.
This agreement will enable Sveriges Riksbank to use T2 for settling large-value payments in Swedish kronor. Migration is targeted for February 2030.
Joining T2 will move Sweden’s large-value payment settlement from a national platform to shared European infrastructure. Sveriges Riksbank and Swedish financial institutions will benefit from investments in security, resilience and technological development that are shared across participating markets, as well as from common European standards. Payments will continue to be settled in Swedish kronor using central bank money.
“Shared payment infrastructure strengthens Europe’s strategic autonomy and supports a more integrated financial system,” said ECB President Christine Lagarde. “This agreement builds on our partnership with Sveriges Riksbank and our joint commitment to safe and efficient payments.”
“By connecting to the European T2 platform for settling payments in Swedish kronor, we can, together with the ECB and other central banks, ensure that the Swedish settlement system becomes an even safer and more efficient payment system in the long run, both in everyday life and in a crisis,” said Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen.
TARGET Services are the Eurosystem’s financial market infrastructure for settling large-value payments, instant payments and securities transactions, and for managing collateral. In addition to payments in euro, T2 already supports large-value payments in Danish kroner. Both Sweden and Denmark use TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) to settle instant payments in Swedish kronor and Danish kroner respectively.
Photos of the signing ceremony will be available on the ECB’s multimedia portal.

Good morning.1 I would like to thank our hosts, the Banco Central do Brasil, the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Financial Stability Institute, for bringing us together. Banking supervisors around the world are tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the banking system. To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Today, I will discuss three ways in which modernizing our supervision and regulatory frameworks can enhance our ability to be effective. 
First, we must learn the appropriate lessons from failures of supervisory effectiveness. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized. 
Second, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must be regularly revisited to keep pace with the evolving financial landscape. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. This is a priority both for the Federal Reserve and our international colleagues, including those on the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the BCBS. 
Third, banking supervisors throughout the Americas must be effective. Our shared history, deeply interconnected economies, and regional financial challenges support alignment of our interests in maintaining strong institutions for supervisory cooperation. ASBA can play a role in that effort. 
These points are closely related. Effective supervision requires sound judgment. Sound judgment must be supported by modern frameworks. And cooperation among supervisors in the Americas supports strengthening both. 
Learning from Banking Failures: Information Must Lead to Action
One of the most valuable responsibilities of any supervisory authority is to learn the right lessons from failure and adjust accordingly. 
The March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), and subsequent discussions about what went wrong and paths for reform, provide a useful case study. Extraordinary measures were taken to address banking system stress in the wake of SVB's failure, and fundamental questions remain regarding the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve System's supervisory function. Earlier reviews of the bank's failure provided important information but did not consider questions about shortcomings in the Federal Reserve's supervisory approach or identify opportunities to address long-standing weaknesses in our supervision. When I became Vice Chair for Supervision, I initiated an independent review of SVB's failure. 
The initial findings of that review released in September were sobering. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure.2 
Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. Yet our supervisory process failed to produce timely and effective action to address them. 
A central lesson is that the failure of supervision was not a failure to obtain information. It was a failure to translate information into timely, decisive action. The review identified a long-standing supervisory problem of consultation without conclusion or action, uncertainty about decisionmaking authority, and a lack of accountability. Supervisors identified concerns, documented weaknesses, and discussed vulnerabilities. But the process did not result in prompt action to require the bank to address material risks that ultimately led to its failure. 
One particularly revealing finding illustrates the problem. Between 2019 and March 2023, supervisors cited 54 supervisory matters that required attention. Yet no finding required SVB to shorten the maturity profile of its securities portfolio or restructure the held-to-maturity book, which were material financial risks that contributed to the bank's failure. Instead, many supervisory findings focused on process concerns. While interest rate risk was discussed, the approach criticized how the bank measured the risk but did not direct the bank to reduce it. 
Supervisors engaged in extensive supervisory activity, produced considerable documentation, and created a substantial record of identified concerns. But the risks that were most material—the risks that affected the bank's financial condition—were not addressed. This experience should encourage every supervisory authority to consider how it measures its own effectiveness. We should not measure success by the number of examinations conducted, findings issued, and reports produced. Instead, we must measure success by whether our work results in the timely identification, mitigation, and remediation of material risks. 
A supervisory organization can be extraordinarily busy without being effective. Excessive process can become a major obstacle to effective supervision. When responsibility is unclear, when decisionmaking authority is fragmented, or when supervisors believe that every judgment must be supported by perfect information, the supervisory process can delay action until it is too late. 
The independent review showed that these organizational and cultural weaknesses can have serious consequences. Supervisory decisions must be grounded in sound analysis, appropriate legal authority, and professional judgment. But those decisions must also be timely. A supervisory judgment that arrives after the opportunity for effective intervention has passed may have little practical value. 
Our goal must be to reach reasonably informed decisions in time to influence outcomes, rather than achieving perfect certainty after the opportunity to act has passed. This lesson becomes even more important as supervisory authorities adopt new technology. Artificial intelligence (or super intelligence), advanced analytics, and other supervisory technologies have the potential to improve the identification of emerging risks and our understanding of complex financial relationships. 
This can provide supervisors access to more information more quickly than ever before. But more information is not necessarily better supervision. The SVB experience should remind us that information alone is not a substitute for judgment and timely action. 
Therefore, our approach must be to modernize supervisory culture while upgrading our supervisory technology. Clear lines of responsibility and decisionmaking authority are imperative. The ultimate measure of successful and effective supervision is the ability to recognize material risks and act effectively while there is still time to influence the outcome. 
Modernizing Our Supervisory and Regulatory Frameworks
Second, we must ensure our regulatory and supervisory frameworks enable the identification of material risks, sound decisionmaking, and supervisory response in a rapidly changing financial system. 
Our priorities should be to ensure supervisors are trained to identify and focus attention on material risks, enable timely decisionmaking and clear accountability, and establish a regulatory framework that encourages innovation without compromising safety and soundness. 
The Federal Reserve is pursuing each of these objectives. 
First, we are modernizing the conduct of supervision. Our Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles refocuses supervision on identifying material risks and taking prompt, proportionate action to address them. 
The principles emphasize risk-focused supervision, tailored to the size, complexity, and risk profile of individual institutions. They call for clearer expectations, greater transparency, and the exercise of sound professional judgment rather than excessive reliance on procedural requirements, checklists, or documentation. They also seek to align examination findings and supervisory ratings more closely with material risks, reduce unnecessary duplication, and streamline the resolution of supervisory concerns. Our objective is not to produce more supervisory findings or more documentation. It is to ensure that supervision identifies the risks that matter most and results in timely action to address them.3 
Second, we are changing how we organize the supervisory function itself. 
The independent review highlighted a fundamental organizational weakness, a mismatch between decisionmaking authority and accountability. The Federal Reserve's supervisory responsibilities have historically been carried out through a complex structure involving the Board, the 12 Reserve Banks, and numerous committees. That structure has not always provided accountability, identified clear lines of responsibility, or supported timely decisions. 
To address these shortcomings, we have begun reorganizing our supervisory function. The reorganization preserves the expertise and relationships of local examination teams while providing clearer lines of accountability through regional leadership. This reorganization is intended to clarify decisionmaking authority, streamline escalation, reduce unnecessary layers of review, and strengthen accountability for supervisory outcomes. We are also examining the role of committees and other internal processes that can cloud responsibility or delay action. 
When supervisors identify a material risk, there should be no ambiguity about who has the authority to act, who is responsible for ensuring that action is taken, and the importance of elevating decisions for prompt action when necessary.4

Deere Reports Net Income of $1.051 Billion for Fourth Quarter, $4.860 Billion for Fiscal Year
 | | ● | Focused execution drives structurally improved results cycle over cycle
 | | ● | North America leads moderate improvement in large ag as global markets begin to stabilize
 | | ● | 2027 company outlook reflects evolving conditions across key end markets
​
MOLINE, Illinois (November 25, 2026) — Deere & Company reported net income of $1.051 billion for the fourth quarter ended November 1, 2026, or $3.89 per share, compared with net income of $1.065 billion, or $3.93 per share, for the quarter ended November 2, 2025. For fiscal year 2026, net income attributable to Deere & Company was $4.860 billion, or $17.95 per share, compared with $5.027 billion, or $18.50 per share, in fiscal 2025.
Worldwide net sales and revenues decreased 2%, to $12.115 billion, for the fourth quarter of 2026 and increased 4%, to $47.704 billion, for the full year. Net sales were $10.514 billion for the quarter and $41.292 billion for the year, compared with $10.579 billion and $38.917 billion in fiscal 2025, respectively.
“Fiscal 2026 proved the strength of our Smart Industrial operating model,” said John May, chairman and chief executive officer of Deere & Company. “Even at cyclical lows, we executed with discipline. Our results are structurally stronger compared with the same point in the last cycle, and we delivered them while sustaining investments and continuing to return capital to shareholders. Those investments are paying off for our customers, as digital engagement and technology utilization continue to expand.”
Company Outlook & Summary
Net income attributable to Deere & Company for fiscal 2027 is forecasted to be in a range of $4.50 to $5.25 billion. The forecast includes an estimated one-time, non-cash pension settlement charge of $0.25 to $0.40 billion associated with a voluntary lump-sum payment option for certain U.S. salaried retirees.
“As we enter fiscal 2027, we’re seeing early signs of improvement in large agriculture, led by North America,” said May. “Given continued uncertainty in key end markets, our outlook reflects a wider range of outcomes. Even so, we’re well positioned to capture the opportunities ahead by delivering solutions that improve our customers’ productivity and profitability, creating lasting value for our shareholders.”

The European Central Bank (ECB) today published its latest study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area (SPACE). The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role.
For the first time since comparable data were collected in 2016,[1] cards were used more often than cash at physical locations, such as shops. In 2026 cards accounted for 45% of transactions, compared with 44% for cash. Mobile payments increased to 9%, from 6% in 2024. 
While payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences remain stable. When paying in a shop, 54% preferred cards or other cashless methods, 22% preferred cash and 23% had no clear preference.
A large majority of respondents attach importance to retaining a choice of payment methods. For 82% of euro area consumers, it is important to have the option to pay digitally, while 62% value the option of paying with cash. Only 3% reported never using cash. 
“Digital means of payment are becoming more important in day-to-day transactions, but choice is what really matters for Europeans,” said Piero Cipollone, member of the ECB’s Executive Board. “The ECB will continue to ensure citizens have the freedom to choose how to pay, by safeguarding cash while preparing for the possible issuance of its digital equivalent, the digital euro.”
Most consumers continue to find it easy to access cash, although the share declined to 85%, from 87% in 2024. Among those who had tried to withdraw cash from an ATM during the previous year, 19% experienced difficulties. In all euro area countries, at least 12% of consumers experienced non-acceptance of mobile or card payments at least once in the month preceding the survey.
The survey covered 51,551 respondents across the euro area. Data were collected in two rounds: the first between 29 September and 27 November 2025, and the second between 16 March and 15 May 2026.
For media queries, please contact Alessandro Speciale, tel.: +49 172 1670791.
 Previous editions of the SPACE study were published in 2019, 2022 and 2024. In 2016 the ECB published a study on the use of cash by households in the euro area (SUCH).

Regulators implement growth-friendly securitisation reforms 
 The Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority have today published revised rules designed to support securitisation’s contribution to economic growth. 
 Published on 
 25 November 2026 
News release
The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have today published revised rules designed to support securitisation’s contribution to economic growth. 
Securitisation allows a firm to divide loans into 'tranches' which have different risk profiles. Investors may buy some or all tranches, providing the firm with funding for further lending, while the interest from the loans pays the investors, who also absorb some of the losses when borrowers do not repay their loans. Securitisation can help firms manage their funding and risk, supporting further lending to businesses and households. 
Today’s changes are designed to make the regulators’ requirements more proportionate and less prescriptive, helping reduce unnecessary costs for firms, while maintaining financial stability. They include: 
Simplifying due diligence and transparency requirements, holding investors and issuers to the same standards of understanding and disclosing risks without being overly prescriptive; 
Introducing more flexible risk retention options, while ensuring firms keep at least 5% of a securitisation's value at risk; 
Allowing some simple and prudent re-securitisations to support firms' funding and liquidity needs, while continuing the ban on the wider practice. 
The reforms are also estimated to reduce industry costs by around £168 million over the next decade while maintaining important safeguards and high standards. 
Phil Evans, Director of Prudential Policy at the Prudential Regulation Authority, said: 
'Securitisation is an important part of a modern financial system. It is obvious that we must never go back to the dangerous practices in place before the great financial crisis, but we shouldn’t go too far the other way either and stifle lending. Today’s final rules strike that balance and should encourage firms to lend more to households and businesses.'
Jon Relleen, Director of Infrastructure and Exchanges at the Financial Conduct Authority, said: 
'Strong capital markets are vital to support economic growth. By simplifying the UK's securitisation regime, we’re reducing unnecessary costs, giving firms and investors greater flexibility, and better reflecting market practice. The changes support more effective markets but crucially also maintain high standards to mitigate potential risks.'
Notes to editors 
Read the full policy statement.
The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework.
This policy statement follows a number of recent PRA and FCA measures aimed at supporting growth, competitiveness and innovation in UK financial services while maintaining financial stability, including, exploring ideas to support the growth of credit unions; simplifying the Senior Managers & Certification regime; and automatically increasing over 100 PRA regulatory thresholds to provide certainty for firms. 
The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. The rules are near-final because the related statutory instrument has been laid by HM Treasury but has not yet been made. The FCA intends to make the final rules shortly after the statutory instrument has been made and does not expect any significant changes to them. The PRA has published final rules at the same time. 
For further details of estimated costs saving, please refer to the cost benefit analyses set out in FCA Consultation Paper CP26/6.

Item 1.01. Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement.
Issuance of Senior Secured Notes
On November 24, 2026, 1011778 B.C. Unlimited Liability Company, an unlimited liability company organized under the laws of British Columbia (the “Issuer”), and New Red Finance, Inc., a Delaware corporation and a direct wholly owned subsidiary of the Issuer (the “Co-Issuer” and, together with the Issuer, the “Issuers”), each a subsidiary of Restaurant Brands International Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of Canada (the “Company”), completed the previously announced public offering (the “Offering”) of $500.0 million aggregate principal amount of their 6.000% Senior Secured Notes due 2031 (the “2031 Notes”) and $500.0 million aggregate principal amount of their 6.400% Senior Secured Notes due 2036 (the “2036 Notes” and, together with the 2031 Notes, the “Notes”), each guaranteed by the Company and the other Guarantors (as defined below). The Offering was made pursuant to an effective shelf registration statement on Form S-3 (Registration No. 333-300072), including a prospectus dated November 16, 2026 and the related prospectus supplement dated November 17, 2026 (the “Prospectus Supplement”).
The Notes were issued pursuant to an indenture, dated as of November 16, 2026 (the “Base Indenture”), by and among the Issuers, the Guarantors and Wilmington Trust, National Association, as trustee (the “Trustee”) and collateral agent (the “Collateral Agent”), as amended and supplemented by the First Supplemental Indenture, dated as of November 24, 2026 (the “First Supplemental Indenture” and together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”), by and among the Issuers, the Guarantors, the Trustee and Collateral Agent.
The Issuers used the proceeds from the Offering to repay a portion of outstanding borrowings under the Issuers’ term loan B facility and to pay fees and expenses in connection therewith and the Offering. The Issuers’ term loan B facility, together with the Issuers’ term loan A facility and revolving credit facility, are referred to herein as the “Senior Secured Credit Facilities.”
Indenture, Notes and Security Agreements 
Maturity and Interest Payment Dates
The 2031 Notes will mature on November 15, 2031, and the 2036 Notes will mature on November 15, 2036. Interest on the Notes will be payable semi-annually, on May 15 and November 15 of each year, commencing on May 15, 2027, to registered holders on May 1 and November 1 each year. 
Note Guarantees
The Notes are senior secured obligations of the Issuers, guaranteed fully and unconditionally, and jointly and severally, (i) on a senior unsecured basis by the Company and (ii) on a first lien senior secured basis by Restaurant Brands International Limited Partnership (the “Partnership”) and certain of its wholly-owned subsidiaries (the Partnership together with such subsidiary guarantors, the “Subsidiary Guarantors”; and together with the Company, the “Guarantors”) that also guarantee the Issuers’ obligations under the Senior Secured Credit Facilities (the “Guarantees”). 
Collateral
In connection with the Offering, the Issuers and the Subsidiary Guarantors entered into a First Lien Security Agreement and a Canadian First Lien Security Agreement, each dated as of November 24, 2026, by and among the Issuer or the Issuers, as applicable, the Subsidiary Guarantors party thereto and the Collateral Agent (collectively, the “Security Agreements”), pursuant to which the Issuers and such Subsidiary Guarantors granted to the Collateral Agent, for the benefit of the holders of the Notes and the other secured parties, a first-priority security interest in the collateral that secures the Issuers’ and the Subsidiary Guarantors’ obligations under the Senior Secured Credit Facilities, subject to certain exceptions and permitted liens.
IG Release Event
The liens on the collateral and the Subsidiary Guarantees (other than that of the Partnership) will be released upon the first date on which (i) the Company achieves a corporate Investment Grade Credit Rating (as defined in the Indenture) from at least two Rating Agencies (as defined in the Indenture) or (ii) the Notes have been assigned an Investment Grade Credit Rating by at least two Rating Agencies after giving effect to the proposed release of the collateral and such Guarantees (an “IG Release Event”). The liens and the Guarantees, are also subject to release in certain other circumstances as described in the Indenture.
Covenants
The Indenture, among other things, limits the ability of the Issuers and certain of their subsidiaries to (1) create or incur certain liens; (2) enter into certain mergers, consolidations and sales of all or substantially all of their assets and (3) after an IG Release Event, enter into certain sale and lease-back transactions, in each case subject to certain qualifications, exceptions and limitations.
Optional Redemption
Prior to October 15, 2031 (the “2031 Notes Par Call Date”), in the case of the 2031 Notes, and August 15, 2036 (the “2036 Notes Par Call Date”), in the case of the 2036 Notes, the Issuers may redeem the Notes, in whole or in part, at any time and from time to time, at a redemption price equal to the greater of (1) a “make-whole” amount calculated as set forth in the Indenture and (2) 100% of the principal amount of the Notes to be redeemed, plus in either case accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to, but excluding, the redemption date. On or after the 2031 Notes Par Call Date or the 2036 Notes Par Call Date, as applicable, the Issuers may redeem some or all of the Notes, at any time and from time to time, at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to, but excluding, the redemption date. The Notes may also be redeemed upon certain changes in tax laws. 
Change of Control
Upon the occurrence of a Change of Control Triggering Event (as defined in the Indenture), holders of the Notes will have the right to require the Issuers to repurchase the Notes at 101% of the principal amount thereof, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to, but excluding, the repurchase date. A Change of Control Triggering Event requires both a Change of Control and a Rating Event, each as defined in the Indenture.
Events of Default
The Indenture also provides for customary events of default which, if any of them occurs, may permit or require the principal amount of, premium, if any, and accrued and unpaid interest, if any, on the Notes to become or to be declared due and payable.
The foregoing descriptions of the Notes, the Guarantees, the Indenture (including the forms of the Notes) and the Security Agreements do not purport to be complete and are qualified in their entirety by the terms of such agreements, which are both incorporated herein by reference and attached hereto as Exhibits 4.1 through 4.6.
Relationships
As more fully described under the caption “Underwriting (Conflicts of Interest)” in the Prospectus Supplement, certain of the underwriters and their respective affiliates have provided, and may in the future provide, a variety of services to the Issuers and to persons and entities with relationships with the Issuers, for which they have received customary fees and expenses. In particular, an affiliate of one of the underwriters acts as administrative agent, collateral agent and as a lender under the Senior Secured Credit Facilities, and affiliates of certain of the other underwriters act as lenders under the Senior Secured Credit Facilities. Affiliates of certain underwriters also act as lenders under the Issuers’ term loan B facility and thus have received a portion of the proceeds from the Offering as a result of the partial repayment of the outstanding borrowings under the Issuers’ term loan B facility.

(e)
Value Creation Awards
On November 20, 2026 (the “Grant Date”), the Board of Directors (the “Board”) of QUALCOMM Incorporated (the “Company”) approved the grant of special long-term equity incentive awards (the “Value Creation Awards” or the “Awards”) to Cristiano Amon, the Company’s President and Chief Executive Officer, and Akash Palkhiwala, the Company’s Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer. The Value Creation Awards were granted under the terms of the Company’s Amended and Restated 2023 Long-Term Incentive Plan (the “Plan”).
The Value Creation Awards have a target value of $50 million for Mr. Amon and $15 million for Mr. Palkhiwala. Each Award will be converted into a target number of performance-based restricted stock units (“PSUs”) determined by dividing each Award’s target value by the average closing price of the Company’s common stock over the 90 trading-day period ending on the trading day prior to the Grant Date (the “Target PSUs”). The Awards are designed to deliver value to the recipients only if exceptional stockholder value is created as part of an unprecedented transformational period for the Company, while supporting the long-term retention of Mr. Amon and Mr. Palkhiwala, both of whom are responsible for executing the Company’s transformation strategy.
Board Rationale
The Value Creation Awards are made in recognition of Mr. Amon’s and Mr. Palkhiwala’s unique value and the criticality of their contributions to the Company’s strategic plans, to motivate and reward creation of exceptional stockholder value, and to further incentivize their long-term retention and dedication.
Following a deliberative process, the Board determined that the Awards best serve the Company’s motivation and retention objectives, aligning with its long-term strategic plan and the interests of its stockholders. The vesting structure of the Awards means that Mr. Amon and Mr. Palkhiwala will only realize the maximum number of shares if they remain with the Company for the entire five-year performance period and the Company experiences substantial increases to its stock price over that time. The backloaded design of the Awards strengthens the alignment of Mr. Amon’s and Mr. Palkhiwala’s interests with the long-term interests of the Company’s stockholders by delivering the significant majority of the Awards’ value to them only if the Company’s stockholders realize significant value as well. Achievement of the highest stock price hurdle would represent a greater than 3x increase in the Company’s stock price from the Grant Date, and, in that scenario, the value of the Awards to Mr. Amon and Mr. Palkhiwala would represent less than one-tenth of one percent of such value creation through the incremental increase in the Company’s market capitalization.
Summary Description
The Value Creation Awards consist of PSUs that can only be earned through the achievement of challenging stock price hurdles during a five-year performance period. The Board designed the Awards to have stock price goals that escalate in magnitude, such that the majority of the PSUs are subject to the highest stock price hurdles. The Board believes this design will strongly align Mr. Amon’s and Mr. Palkhiwala’s pay opportunities with the Company’s long-term strategic plan and stockholders’ interests. Moreover, the stock price hurdles must be met within predefined performance periods, with the first two tranches linked to performance during Years 1 to 3 and the final three tranches linked to performance during Years 3 to 5, incentivizing Mr. Amon and Mr. Palkhiwala to drive superior performance consistently over the entire five years. The Awards are also subject to a service-based vesting condition requiring Mr. Amon’s and Mr. Palkhiwala’s continued service with the Company through the end of the applicable service vesting period in order to receive any shares issued under the Awards, even if the applicable stock price goals have already been achieved. Additionally, all PSUs earned will be subject to a one-year holding period following the vesting of the Awards.
The Awards are not part of Mr. Amon’s or Mr. Palkhiwala’s regular annual compensation. The Board intends that the Awards be a one-time special equity award and that, absent extraordinary or unforeseen circumstances, Mr. Amon and Mr. Palkhiwala will not receive any other special equity award (i.e., an equity award outside of their regular annual compensation) for the duration of the performance period.
Stock Price Hurdles and Payout Schedule
The following table shows the percentage of Target PSUs that may be earned for each tranche of the Value Creation Awards. In order to earn the applicable number of PSUs for each tranche set forth below, the average closing price of the Company’s common stock over any 90 trading-day period during the specified portion of the performance period applicable to such tranche (each, a “Performance Window”) must equal or exceed the applicable stock price hurdle. If a stock price hurdle is achieved either before or after the applicable Performance Window, the tranche will be forfeited. 
 | | | | | | | | | | | | 
 | | Performance Window (1) | PSUs Earned (2) | Stock Price Hurdle 
 | Tranche 1 | Years 1 & 2 | 20% of Target PSUs | $250
 | Tranche 2 | Years 2 & 3 | 40% of Target PSUs | $300
 | Tranche 3 | Years 3 & 4 | 60% of Target PSUs | $350
 | Tranche 4 | Years 4 & 5 | 80% of Target PSUs | $400

(1)The Performance Window represents the number of years following the Grant Date. For example, Year 1 represents the period from the Grant Date to the first anniversary thereof, and Year 2 represents the period from the first anniversary of the Grant Date to the second anniversary thereof. 
(2)The PSUs earned in each tranche are independent of each other tranche, such that if all stock price hurdles are achieved during the applicable Performance Windows, the maximum number of PSUs earned would be 300% of Target PSUs.
Service Requirement and Termination Provisions
The service requirement for the first two tranches will be satisfied on the third anniversary of the Grant Date, and the service requirement for the final three tranches will be satisfied on the fifth anniversary of the Grant Date, in each case, subject to Mr. Amon’s and Mr. Palkhiwala’s continued service with the Company through such anniversary. 
If Mr. Amon’s or Mr. Palkhiwala’s service terminates prior to the vesting of any tranche of the Awards, such tranche will be forfeited, except that if Mr. Amon or Mr. Palkhiwala experiences a Qualified Termination (as defined in the Company’s Executive Officer Severance Plan) after the stock price hurdle of a tranche has been satisfied but before the applicable service vesting requirement has been satisfied, such tranche will vest upon such termination of service. The Awards do not include the retirement provisions that apply to Mr. Amon’s and Mr. Palkhiwala’s regular annual PSU awards, and Mr. Amon and Mr. Palkhiwala will not be eligible to retain any portion of the Awards solely on the basis of their retirement.
If a Change in Control (as defined in the Plan) occurs during the performance period, any tranche for which the stock price hurdle would be achieved based on the value of the per-share consideration received by the Company’s stockholders will be deemed vested, and the remainder of the Awards will be forfeited.

Subject to FDA Approval, Amgen Will Launch ABP 206 in the U.S. on October 1, 2028
THOUSAND OAKS, Calif. (November 24, 2026) – Amgen (NASDAQ: AMGN) today announced that it has reached a settlement agreement with Bristol-Myers Squibb Company, E. R. Squibb & Sons, L.L.C., and Ono Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (collectively, “BMS”) to resolve the existing U.S. patent litigation related to ABP 206, Amgen’s investigational biosimilar to OPDIVO® (nivolumab). ABP 206 is a monoclonal antibody that binds to programmed death protein 1 (PD-1).
The settlement allows Amgen to launch its biosimilar to OPDIVO in the U.S. prior to the expiration of patents that could have otherwise been asserted against this medicine. The company will launch ABP 206 in the U.S. on October 1, 2028, subject to U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval. The company’s Biologics License Application (BLA) for ABP 206 has been submitted to and accepted for review by the FDA. The agency is expected to take action on the application by the end of 2026.
“Advancing innovative medicines and supporting a competitive biosimilars marketplace both play important roles in creating a more sustainable health care system,” said Murdo Gordon, executive vice president, Global Markets and Policy at Amgen. “This agreement creates a pathway for timely biosimilar competition, with the potential to generate savings for patients and the U.S. health care system. Our continued investment in biosimilars reflects our long-term commitment to bringing high-quality medicines to people living with the toughest diseases around the world.”
The terms of the settlement agreement are confidential.
About ABP 206
ABP 206 is an investigational biosimilar to OPDIVO® (nivolumab), a monoclonal antibody that binds to the receptor protein called programmed death protein 1 (PD-1). OPDIVO® is a registered trademark of Bristol-Myers Squibb Company.

The Company has entered into an equity purchase agreement (“EPA”) with Piedmont Healthcare to sell our wholly-owned subsidiary which owns and operates Aiken Regional Medical Centers (“ARMC”), consisting of a 211-bed acute care hospital, an integrated 62-bed behavioral health care pavilion facility, and certain related assets, located in Aiken, South Carolina. The sale price is approximately $500 million, subject to certain adjustments, and the EPA is subject to customary closing conditions, including applicable regulatory and governmental approvals. The closing is scheduled to occur the later of: (i) five business days following satisfaction of all closing conditions, including the receipt of all regulatory and governmental approvals; or (ii) January 31, 2027. 
The real estate assets of ARMC are currently leased from Universal Health Realty Income Trust (the “Trust”) pursuant to a lease that is scheduled to expire in December 2033. The EPA requires that such assets be acquired by ARMC from the Trust immediately prior to closing. As permitted pursuant to the terms of the lease, we have the right to acquire the leased property from the Trust by offering the Trust potential substitution properties with aggregate appraised fair market value substantially equal to the appraised fair market value of leased property and providing the Trust with a yield (i.e., annual return on its equity in such property) equal to that provided by the ARMC leased property. Any substitution transaction between us and the Trust will be subject to, and effective upon, the closing of the EPA. 
We expect to submit our proposal to the Trust by no later than early January 2027. Upon receipt, the proposal will be reviewed and evaluated by management and the Board of Trustees of the Trust. All transactions with the Company must be approved by a majority of the Independent Trustees of the Trust. We can provide no assurance that we will ultimately agree on a property substitution with the Trust in connection with the ARMC leased assets. Daniel E. Pinto appointed to the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee 
 Daniel E. Pinto has been appointed as an external member of the Financial Policy Committee. 
 Published on 
 24 November 2026 
News release
The Chancellor of the Exchequer has appointed Daniel E. Pinto as an external member of the Financial Policy Committee (FPC). 
Mr Pinto has over 40 years of experience in financial services, including in senior leadership roles across global financial markets, most recently as Vice Chairman at JPMorgan Chase. He will serve a 3-year term, which will begin on 4 January 2027. His appointment fills the position held by Jonathan Hall, who will step down from the Committee on 31 December 2026. 
Economic Secretary to the Treasury, Lucy Rigby, said: 
“The Financial Policy Committee plays a vital role in protecting and enhancing the stability of the UK’s financial system. Daniel Pinto's significant experience across global financial markets will be valuable for the Committee’s work. I would also like to thank Jon Hall for his contribution to the Committee over the past six years.” 
Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England, said: 
“I am delighted that Daniel will be joining the Financial Policy Committee. He brings an exceptional breadth of international experience and a perspective that will add greatly to the Committee’s discussions. My thanks also go to Jon for his dedicated service over the years.”
Daniel Pinto, said:
“I am honored to join the Financial Policy Committee and look forward to working with the Governor and my fellow members. The resilience and stability of the financial system are critical to a strong economy, and I look forward to contributing to the Committee’s important work.”
About Daniel E. Pinto 
Mr Pinto has more than 40 years’ experience in financial services, most recently as Vice Chairman of JPMorgan Chase. He previously served as the firm’s President and Chief Operating Officer and as CEO of its Corporate & Investment Bank, having held a range of senior leadership roles across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and emerging markets. He has also served on a number of international financial services and corporate boards.
About the Appointments Process 
The appointment follows a fair and open competition in line with the Governance Code on Public Appointments, and is subject to pre-commencement scrutiny by the Treasury Select Committee on 15 December 2026. 
Mr Pinto has confirmed that he has not engaged in any significant party political activity in the last five years. A panel interviewed a number of candidates and made recommendations to the Chancellor, which informed his decision. 
About the Financial Policy Committee 
The FPC is the UK’s macroprudential regulator: its objective is to protect and enhance the stability of the UK’s financial system by identifying, monitoring and addressing systemic risks. 
The FPC has thirteen members. Six of them are Bank of England staff: the Governor, four Deputy Governors and the Executive Director for Financial Stability Strategy and Risk. 
There are also five external members who are selected from outside the Bank for their experience and expertise in financial services. 
The Committee also includes the Chief Executive of the Financial Conduct Authority and a non-voting member from HM Treasury.

CONSUMER PRICE INDEX - OCTOBER 2026
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October 
after rising 0.6 percent in September, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. 
The index for shelter rose 0.3 percent in October, accounting for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. 
The food index increased 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home 
index increased 0.5 percent. The index for energy increased 0.7 percent over the month following a 5.2-percent increase 
in September. 
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. Indexes that 
increased over the month include recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance, household furnishings and operations, 
and education. Conversely, the index for used cars and trucks and the index for communication were among the small number 
of major indexes that decreased in October.
